newsitem.title: INDIA: Introspective India appeals for corruption crusade.
newsitem.headline: Introspective India appeals for corruption crusade.

text.p: A brooding India marked half a century of freedom on Friday with patriotic pageantry overshadowed by sombre calls for a national crusade against the evil of corruption.
Taking a page from Mahatma Gandhi, India's leaders appealed to citizens to tackle graft with a mass campaign of civil disobedience, just as freedom fighters combatted two centuries of British rule.

"We have to build a mass movement in which all can join so that corruption in politics, politicians and public life must end," Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said in a solemn speech from the sandstone ramparts of Delhi's Red Fort.
"It is eating into the country's vitals like termites."
As Gujral spoke, hundreds of school children sat in neat rows wearing crisp sashes bearing the saffron, white and green emblem of India's 50th anniversary of independence.
"Long live India!" they shouted in unison when Gujral finished, thrusting their fists into the sultry monsoon air.

"A widespread national movement is needed to cleanse the system," President K.R. Narayanan told a special session of parliament that started at the stroke of midnight -- exactly 50 years after the dawn of Indian freedom.
The soul-searching reflected the nation's deeply mixed feelings on the anniversary of independence from colonial rule.

Invoking Gandhi and the first prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru, the country's leaders pointed proudly to India's achievements: self-sufficiency in food, a vibrant democracy, industrial and technological progress.
But the watershed anniversary stirred a bout of self-recrimination as leaders recalled illiteracy, poverty, population growth, environmental degradation and, above all, corruption in public life.
"A tryst yet unredeemed," The Hindu said in a headline recalling Nehru's words, "a tryst with destiny".
"We had pledged to 'wipe every tear from every eye' at the dawn of freedom," The Pioneer said, repeating Gandhi's pledge. "Tears have welled up in many more eyes over the past 50 years."
Surveys show a series of corruption scandals involving politicians and bureaucrats has sapped the public's morale.

"As the years have gone by, the dream has turned into a nightmare; idealism has been replaced by cynicism; and the pursuit of power has blinded politicians," The Times of India said in a front page editorial.
A former leader of Gujral's Janata Dal party, Laloo Prasad Yadav, has been indicted in a $280-million scandal that has rocked the prime minister's coalition. Yadav says he is innocent.
Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao has been charged in two criminal corruption cases. He denies any wrongdoing.
Gujral reached out to women in his 90-minute nationally televised address, vowing to protect girls against discrimination and promote women in politics.
He announced that the government would bar doctors from revealing whether a foetus is a girl or boy, and unveiled a special fund for girls in poor families.

More boys than girls are born in India, where social workers say women sometimes choose abortion to avoid having a girl child who could later weigh on the family's finances because of the heavy cost of dowry.
In a reminder of the separatist tensions that persist in India, six people were killed in the rebellious northeast in scattered incidents amid a general strike in four states.
Separatist militants blew up a bridge in the central section of Assam state and set on fire a small railway station on the main track connecting the region with the rest of India.
